newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba's Welteke, Zeitler clash over EMU criteria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba's Welteke, Zeitler clash over EMU criteria.

text.p: Two Bundesbank council members clashed on Friday over how Germany should approach the Maastricht criteria for Europe's single currency.

While both Ernst Welteke and Franz-Christoph Zeitler stressed the need for credibility and sustainability in progess toward European economic and monetary union (EMU), they gave starkly different views on how this could be achieved.

Zeitler, president of the Bavarian state central bank, said a strict interpretation of EMU entry rules was critical, saying that a lax approach to the Maastricht reference targets would threaten the euro's stability.

In the summary of a speech, Zeitler said the EMU deficit criterion, which calls on euro hopefuls to reduce budget deficits to at most three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, should be taken seriously.

Zeitler, who has previously taken a hard line against using accounting tricks to reduce budget deficits, said the three percent target had become an international benchmark by which to judge fiscal policy and stability.
"Credibility in the fulfilment of fiscal criteria is imprtant for the long-term stability and a long-term acceptance of the euro," Zeitler said.

But Welteke, who is president of the Hessen state central bank, criticised talk of Germany not meeting EMU rules, saying that the 3.0 percent deficit reference should not be seen as the be-all and end-all for joining EMU.
"Contrary to the impression that is often raised in Germany 3.0 percent is not a knockout criterion for participation in monetary union," Welteke told an EMU conference in Wiesbaden.
Welteke's comments were consistent with his previously stated view that the EMU's guiding Maastricht Treaty provided for some leeway on budget criteria.

Speculation about Germany's fiscal fitness for the single currency has heightened again after the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said in a report on Thursday that Germany and France, seen as key participants in the euro, would both exceed the three percent deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio in 1997.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, speaking on German television late on Thursday, said he was not prepared to become embroiled in a "discussion of about decimal points" in EMU criteria.
Taking a similar line, Welteke, speaking at an EMU conference in Wiesbaden, said suggestions that Germany would fail to meet Maastricht criteria were "absolute humbug".

He said Germany already met criteria on monetary stability, central bank independence and low inflation, and that it had the possibility if fulfilling the fiscal criteria, which anyway should not be seen as point-landing targets.
"The issue of sustainability is the critical factor," Welteke said.

But Zeitler warned against a "generous" reading of the Maastricht treaty, stressing that a stability pact, due to be signed at an EU summit in Amsterdam next week, offered little space for loose fiscal policy.

The pact, which is designed to ensure budgetary discilpine after the planned birth of the euro in 1999, envisages sanctions against countries which breach reference limits, he said, and such details left no room for interpretation "after the decimal point".
